classification.tone: Propulsive, paranoid, emotionally earnest, and increasingly tragic before landing on cathartic found-family uplift

evaluation.positioning_hook: A bullied teen discovers she’s a shapeshifting lab experiment in a town-wide coverup, and the only way to survive is to become everyone else first.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, easy-to-sell engine: a teen discovers hidden powers, a corporate coverup, and a body-morphing survival game. The emotional lane broadens it beyond genre fans, especially through Ava’s self-worth arc and the mother-daughter/found-family finish.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the cold open with the girl running from armed pursuers, then sharpens fast when the shapeshifting is revealed in the alley and the town coverup kicks in. By the time Ava is pulled into the company’s orbit, the story engine is clear and specific.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ava has a strong internal contradiction: smart, self-conscious, morally awake, and desperate to matter. June, Shannon, Priscilla, and Madison all add distinct energy, though the script’s strongest character charge lives in Ava and the Ava/Madison identity collision.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The body-changing mechanic is used in a fresh, story-driving way, especially the identity confusion between Ava and Madison and the way touch becomes both power and danger. The script also commits to a big, weird emotional swing: teen insecurity, biotech conspiracy, and existential identity horror all in one lane.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps escalating: escape, discovery, school confrontation, mall chase, lab reveal, identity reversal, and final showdown. Each major sequence turns the screw on Ava’s understanding of herself and the company’s control, so the read stays active and forward-moving.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a girl who thinks she’s Ava but is actually Madison, with memory suppression and body-copying tied to touch, gives the premise a memorable emotional and conceptual twist. It feels like a genre premise that could only exist in this exact form once the identity reveal lands.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The small-town setting, school ecosystem, mall, ranch house, and secret lab all feel usable and connected, with the company’s presence visibly bleeding into daily life. The world is strongest when it shows how a biotech operation can hide inside ordinary civic spaces and social media noise.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct tonal blend: teen embarrassment, paranoid thriller mechanics, body-horror mutation, and sincere emotional pleading. Scenes like the cafeteria reveal, the mall identity scramble, and the final pendant beat give it a recognizable voice rather than a generic genre surface.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the chase mechanics, the script is really about identity, class resentment, maternal love, and who gets to become powerful. The Ava/Madison split and the company’s moral rot suggest deeper thematic layers that reward a second look.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ava and June are a strong core, Shannon gives the teen world texture, and the Ava/Madison relationship becomes the emotional center of the back half. The supporting company figures are functional and vivid, with Priscilla, Wilma, Mills, and Wolcott each carrying a clear dynamic.

casting_characteristics: Teen female lead with strong emotional range
Multiple adult performers must plausibly play multiple identities/forms
Some roles require physicality and action comfort

notable_requirements: Small-town streets, high school, mall, ranch house, warehouse, secret lab, forest road, and wooded areas
Contained practical locations with one primary lab build

technical.vfx_details: Frequent body-shift transformations, skin bubbling/mutation, identity swaps, and a few stylized flash-cut memory effects.
technical.sfx_needs: Foam spray effects, burns, fire sequence, gunfire, taser/cattle prod beats, practical injury and transformation makeup.

rights_flags.detail: Eric Huntington is a fictional billionaire character, but the script references the New York Times as a plot point and uses real-world media behavior.
Trader Joe’s, CNN, TikTok, Google, Target, and Panda Express are named on the page.
Indiana Jones is referenced in dialogue.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming or premium-cable sci-fi thriller lane with theatrical-capable genre packaging
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: festival-to-platform or genre-theatrical with strong streamer afterlife

cost.note: The story is mostly contemporary and contained, but the transformation effects, lab build, fire sequence, and chase coverage push it above micro-budget.

cast.note: The script needs a strong teen lead, a credible mother, and performers who can play multiple forms/identities across the shapeshifting conceit.

location.note: It moves through a town, school, mall, house, warehouse, forest, and secret lab, but the footprint stays within a manageable contemporary footprint.

content.note: There is violence, child endangerment, body horror, gunplay, and some intense peril, but the material still sits in a broadly accessible thriller lane.

rights.note: Several prominent brands and a named pop-culture reference appear, but there is no major life-rights or franchise dependency.

strengths.what_it_means: A producer can pitch this in one breath: a teen discovers she’s a shapeshifting lab experiment and gets trapped inside a corporate identity theft scheme. That kind of clean, high-contrast premise is exactly what gets buyers to lean in and actors to ask for the script.
strengths.evidence: Cold open chase, alley transformation, and the later reveal that the town’s company is covering up escaped shapeshifters.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ava is built for an actor.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives a young actress insecurity, intelligence, moral clarity, panic, and physical transformation all in one part. That is the kind of showcase that can launch a new face or reframe an actor already known for teen material.
strengths.evidence: Ava’s crush humiliation at Sammy’s, her confrontation with Priscilla in class, and the sequence where she becomes Christy, Grandma, Tomas, and Eric.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The body-swap mechanic has emotional stakes.
strengths.what_it_means: This is not just a gimmick; touch becomes intimacy, contamination, and identity theft at once. That gives the movie a commercial engine with thematic weight, which is the sweet spot for genre buyers looking for something smarter than a standard chase movie.
strengths.evidence: Ava touching Christy, Wilma, Priscilla, Mills, and finally Eric, each contact changing the story’s emotional direction.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The mother-daughter dynamic carries the back half.
strengths.what_it_means: June is not just support; she becomes the emotional counterweight and action partner, which widens the audience beyond teen genre viewers. That gives the project a built-in adult anchor for buyers who want a thriller with family heat, not just concept mechanics.
strengths.evidence: June’s reveal as a shifter, the car escape, the mall sequence, and the final alliance with Ava and Madison.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The villainy is corporate, not cartoonish.
strengths.what_it_means: Priscilla, Wolcott, and the company apparatus feel like a real machine with lawyers, investors, media manipulation, and a public-facing cover story. That makes the movie feel current and exportable, because the threat is institutional and recognizable rather than purely fantastical.
strengths.evidence: The school visit, the hotline messaging, the investor Zoom, the fake reporter call, and the settlement language.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending lands on found family.
strengths.what_it_means: The final emotional turn gives the movie a satisfying aftertaste: the girls, the mom, the dog, and even the damaged shifters form a new unit. That kind of catharsis helps a genre title travel beyond horror/thriller fans into broader audience conversation.
strengths.evidence: Real Ava, Madison, June, Shannon, Mills, and Murray driving away together after the lab burns.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world has a strong visual engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The script keeps finding cinematic set pieces: woods, roadside chaos, mall disguise play, sterile lab horror, and a fire-driven climax. That gives a director and production designer a lot to build around without needing a giant fantasy world.
strengths.evidence: The gully chase, mall transformation sequence, secret lab reveal, and final inferno.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, commercial sci-fi thriller with a real identity: a teen body-shifter story that turns self-esteem, class resentment, and corporate conspiracy into one propulsive engine. The script has a clean hook, a showcase lead role, and a finale that pays off as both genre spectacle and emotional release.

lead_characters.name: Madison / Ava Mayfield
lead_characters.hook: A smart, self-conscious teen who thinks she’s an ordinary girl named Ava, but is actually Madison — a traumatized shapeshifter whose identity has been buried under memory suppression and someone else’s life. She’s funny, observant, morally stubborn, and emotionally raw, with a body that keeps betraying her and a heart that keeps trying to do the right thing anyway.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Saoirse Ronan in Lady Bird and Florence Pugh in Midsommar — a role where interior shame, wit, and panic all live in the same frame. A young actress gets to play insecurity, physical transformation, moral awakening, and a final identity reclamation, which is exactly the kind of part that can announce a star.

lead_characters.name: June Bennett
lead_characters.hook: A blue-collar, sharp-tongued single mom who looks like she’s barely holding life together, then reveals she’s tougher, smarter, and more dangerous than anyone expects. She’s practical, funny, emotionally direct, and deeply protective, with a lived-in weariness that turns into action when her kid is threatened.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Toni Collette in Hereditary or Patricia Arquette in Medium — a mother role that can pivot from everyday exhaustion to ferocious protectiveness without losing humanity. Mid-career actresses who want a role with both domestic texture and action authority will chase this immediately.

lead_characters.name: Shannon
lead_characters.hook: Ava’s best friend is the movie’s social ballast: warm, funny, a little more grounded in the teen ecosystem, and the first person to make Ava feel seen without demanding she perform. She gives the story normal teenage oxygen even as the plot goes off the rails.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of best-friend part that has the easy, lived-in charm of Beanie Feldstein in Booksmart’s social orbit — a role that gets laughs, loyalty, and real emotional utility. Young actors who can play comic timing and sincere friendship will want it because it makes them memorable without needing the whole movie.

lead_characters.name: Priscilla Jones
lead_characters.hook: A polished private-security operator who can switch from corporate calm to hard-edged control in a beat. She’s not a cackling villain; she’s a professional who believes she’s managing a catastrophe, which makes her more unsettling.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of authority role that gave Carrie Coon in The Leftovers or Rebecca Ferguson in Mission: Impossible a chance to command a room with intelligence and menace. Character actresses who can play competence, pressure, and moral compromise will see a juicy, scene-stealing lane here.

lead_characters.name: Wilma
lead_characters.hook: A company nurse with a bright, watchful surface and a hidden capacity for manipulation, empathy, and damage. She’s one of the story’s most interesting doubles: caring enough to be trusted, compromised enough to be dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the layered, shifting work Elisabeth Moss does in The Handmaid’s Tale — warmth on the surface, calculation underneath, and a body that becomes part of the performance. It’s a great fit for actors who like playing ambiguity without losing emotional clarity.

lead_characters.name: Jamieson
lead_characters.hook: A blunt, security-first enforcer who reads like a guy who has spent his life being told to keep things contained. He’s physically imposing, procedural, and just human enough to feel like he’s following orders rather than inventing evil.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of hard-edged utility role that gives an actor the grounded menace of Shea Whigham in any number of pressure-cooker thrillers. Character actors who can make a gun-and-radio guy feel real will want the efficiency and authority of this part.

lead_characters.name: Mills
lead_characters.hook: A younger company guard with a Marine background and a conscience that keeps leaking through the job. He’s the story’s most usable inside man: physically capable, morally conflicted, and not fully committed to the machine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Adam Driver in BlacKkKlansman or Jesse Plemons in a moral-pressure role — a man whose stillness hides a conscience the audience can read. Actors who can play restraint, regret, and sudden action will see a strong supporting turn here.

lead_characters.name: Wolcott
lead_characters.hook: The scientist-architect of the whole operation, coldly convinced he is building the future and entitled to the bodies he ruins along the way. He’s not flashy; he’s worse than that — he’s rational, self-justifying, and intellectually arrogant.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of prestige-villain role that gives an actor the chilling certainty of Michael Keaton in Spotlight or Bryan Cranston in a darker register — a man who believes his own logic. Veteran actors who want authority, intelligence, and moral rot in one package will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Christy
lead_characters.hook: The beautiful, athletic girl Ava envies is not just a crush object; she’s a mirror for Ava’s insecurity and a body that becomes part of the identity game. She functions as both teen aspiration and transformation template.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the glossy, charged presence of a teen standout in a prestige genre film — the sort of part that can turn a newcomer into a face casting directors remember. It’s especially attractive to young actors who can play physical confidence and emotional distance.

lead_characters.name: Liam
lead_characters.hook: Ava’s crush is sweet, athletic, and slightly unreadable, which makes him feel like a real teen boy instead of a stock love interest. He becomes a key emotional trigger and, later, a body the story can weaponize for identity confusion.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of teen male role that gives an actor the understated appeal of Noah Centineo in a more genre-forward lane — charm, mystery, and a chance to become the emotional object of the lead’s attention. Young actors who want a part with both romantic and plot utility will want it.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.hook: The old man at the center of the other shifter’s bond is fragile, haunted, and unexpectedly tender, but also capable of obsession and violence when survival takes over. He’s the story’s most tragic mirror: a damaged person who keeps trying to protect the one person he has left.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the emotional and physical range of Anthony Hopkins in The Father crossed with a body-performance challenge — age, vulnerability, menace, and love all in one. A veteran actor looking for a late-career showcase with real transformation work would be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Madison
lead_characters.hook: The little girl at the center of the body-horror conceit is terrified, hungry, and emotionally stranded, but also startlingly resilient. She’s the original self buried under the Ava identity, and the movie’s deepest innocence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child role that can be played with the haunting directness of Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project — a child performance that carries the emotional truth of the entire movie. It’s a rare part for a young performer because it’s not decorative; it’s the story’s soul.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a body-horror thriller with real heart and a teen emotional center.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Mid-career indie genre directors or first/second-feature filmmakers coming out of festival shorts, especially those who already work in psychological horror, elevated sci-fi, or performance-forward thrillers. This material rewards directors who like clean visual rules, intimate character pressure, and practical set pieces that can escalate into emotional payoff.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a chance to stage transformations as character beats, not just effects, and to build suspense through identity confusion rather than constant exposition. It’s especially attractive to filmmakers who can make a contained contemporary world feel cinematic without needing a giant VFX canvas.

buyer_appeal.lane: Streaming-friendly elevated sci-fi thriller with theatrical genre upside
buyer_appeal.detail: The script can be packaged around one breakout teen lead plus a strong adult mother role, which lowers the need for a giant ensemble or franchise-level star stack. The contained contemporary footprint, recognizable teen setting, and body-morph hook make it exportable and easy to market in the genre lane buyers already know how to sell.

considerations.area: The Ava/Madison reveal drives the whole back half.
considerations.detail: The identity reversal is the movie’s biggest swing and it pays off as a genuine emotional turn. One lever would be to keep seeding Madison’s buried self a little earlier in the Ava sections so the reveal feels inevitable as well as surprising.

considerations.area: The company mythology arrives in waves.
considerations.detail: The script does a lot of smart work revealing the operation through school visits, hotline messaging, the mall, and the lab, but the audience is also tracking a lot of moving parts. A next pass could clarify the rules of touch, memory, and foam a touch earlier so the later reversals land with even more force.

considerations.area: The supporting cast is built for a contained budget.
considerations.detail: The story lives mostly in contemporary locations with a manageable number of principal players, which keeps it in a producible feature lane. That makes it a strong candidate for streamer or specialty financing, especially if the transformation effects are designed with a disciplined visual approach.

considerations.area: The mall and lab sequences carry the biggest production lift.
considerations.detail: The mall chase, multiple identity changes, and the fire-heavy climax are the most effects- and stunt-forward sections. A simplification lever would be to protect the emotional beats while keeping the number of distinct transformation beats in those sequences tightly chosen.

considerations.area: The teen social world is doing real work.
considerations.detail: Ava, Shannon, Liam, and Christy give the movie a teen ecosystem that makes the sci-fi premise feel grounded in recognizable social pain. A next pass could keep that world active even in the middle stretch so the genre plot never floats away from the emotional stakes.
